chapter_title: The DRY Principle: Don't Repeat Yourself

screens.title: The DRY Principle: Don't Repeat Yourself
screens.subtitle: Make every piece of knowledge in your system single and authoritative.

narration.text: In this lesson we will explore the Don't Repeat Yourself principle and why it matters in day-to-day software work. DRY says every piece of knowledge in a system should have one clear authoritative representation. That includes obvious code duplication but also duplicated data, documentation, and manual processes. When knowledge is repeated, change becomes risky: updating one copy and missing another creates inconsistencies and bugs. You will see concrete refactorings, a before-and-after coding demo, and a hands-on refactor exercise for configuration loading. We'll also learn how to spot duplication beyond simple copy‑paste and how to balance DRY with practical concerns like readability and future divergence. Expect concrete patterns — extracting validation functions, centralizing configuration, or creating middleware — and a discussion of a common pitfall: premature abstraction. As you move through the lesson, think of a recent bug or customer complaint that came from inconsistent rules. That real example will help you spot where knowledge is repeated in your codebase and where a single, well-defined source of truth would reduce errors.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Make knowledge authoritative: centralize rules, data, and process so changes are implemented once and propagate reliably.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this lesson

narration.text: By the end of this lesson you will be able to recognize and remove repeated knowledge across a system. First, you'll understand the DRY principle: why a single authoritative representation of knowledge prevents divergence and bugs. Second, you'll identify duplication in its many forms: not just identical code, but repeated configuration, documentation, or manual steps. Third, you'll apply practical refactorings: extracting validation, centralizing configuration loaders, and using middleware to consolidate cross-cutting concerns. Fourth, you'll weigh trade-offs and avoid premature abstraction by asking whether repeated code actually represents the same piece of knowledge. These objectives matter because change is constant in software. When rules live in one place, updates are safer and audits are easier. For example, centralizing email validation into a shared validator guarantees that registration, profile updates, and password resets behave the same way. Keep the question in mind: does this repetition represent the same rule or only a superficial similarity? That question will guide whether you refactor now or wait for clearer evidence.

screens.title: What DRY Really Means
screens.subtitle: Every piece of knowledge must have a single authoritative representation.

narration.text: DRY is often misread as simply "don't copy‑paste code," but its true scope is broader. The principle says every piece of knowledge in a system — a business rule, a data derivation, or an operational procedure — should be represented in a single place. That authoritative representation is the one source you update when the rule changes. A concrete example: calculating a discount rate for a purchase should be defined once and referenced wherever pricing occurs. If you implement that calculation in three different modules, a change to the rule forces three edits and increases the chance of forgetting one. A common misconception is to equate syntactic similarity with shared knowledge. Two functions can look alike yet encode different intent. For instance, identical sorting logic applied to customer names versus product IDs may diverge later; premature abstraction would couple those futures and create a leaky abstraction. The practical advice is to identify the knowledge first, then choose a focused, readable abstraction: a validation function, a configuration key, or a small service. Ask: is this repetition the same rule, or only coincidence? That question steers safe refactoring.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: DRY targets knowledge duplication, not merely repeated text. Centralize intent, not only syntax.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › What DRY Means

Every piece of knowledge gets one home

DRY is about intent: the authoritative representation of business rules, algorithms, and processes.

Explanation and examples
  • Authoritative representation: define the rule once and reference it everywhere.
  • Example: a single discount calculation prevents inconsistent pricing across modules.
  • Data duplication example: storing both birthdate and age creates two sources of truth.
  • Documentation duplication: README versus wiki can drift if one is primary and the other is not.
Key Takeaway

Focus on centralizing the knowledge, not just removing repeated lines of code.

Analogy and misconception

Analogy: a recipe referenced by multiple cooks keeps the instructions consistent. Misconception: identical code always represents the same knowledge — not always. Ask if the similarity is intentional or coincidental.

Common Mistake

Abstraction before you understand the knowledge often makes code harder to change later.

screens.title: Forms of Duplication
screens.subtitle: Code, data, documentation, and process duplication explained

narration.text: Duplication shows up in several ways beyond copy‑pasted code. The first is syntactic duplication: identical or near‑identical code blocks. This is the easiest to spot and often straightforward to refactor. Second is knowledge duplication: the same business rule implemented in multiple places, possibly with slight variations. For example, email validation implemented separately in three forms is knowledge duplication, because the validation rule should be one authoritative routine. Third is data duplication: storing both derived and source values, like keeping age and birthdate, which invites divergence when time passes. Fourth is process duplication: manual steps repeated by engineers — think of repeated deployment steps that should be automated. Each form has a different remedy: syntactic duplication often benefits from simple extraction; knowledge duplication needs careful design of the authoritative representation; data duplication may require normalization or derivation; process duplication suggests automation. A misconception is treating all duplication identically. Practical inspection looks for the underlying rule. When you see repeated behavior, ask: what knowledge is being expressed and where should that knowledge live? Forms of Duplication means not all duplication is code copying; identify whether the repetition is syntax, knowledge, data, or process to choose the right fix.. In practical terms, code, data, documentation, and process duplication explained. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Forms of Duplication

Forms of Duplication

Identify what is duplicated to apply the right refactor.

Comparison table
Syntactic duplication: identical functions or blocks. Fix: extract shared function or helper.
Knowledge duplication: same business rule in multiple places. Fix: single authoritative routine or module.
Data duplication: storing derived data redundantly. Fix: store canonical value and derive others.
Process duplication: manual repeated steps. Fix: automate with scripts or CI pipelines.
Example scenarios
  • Email validation in three forms → knowledge duplication → extract to shared validator.
  • Age and birthdate stored separately → data duplication → derive age from birthdate.
  • Copying SQL queries with small edits → knowledge duplication of access patterns → centralize in a repository.
Pro Tip

Name the piece of knowledge clearly before refactoring; the name becomes the authoritative contract.

screens.title: A Refactoring Process to Remove Duplication
screens.subtitle: How to discover, extract, and verify a central representation safely

narration.text: A safe refactoring to remove duplication follows a clear process. First, detect repetition and name the knowledge: write a short sentence describing the rule or behavior you see repeated. Second, write tests that capture existing behavior so you can detect regressions. Testing gives you confidence during extraction. Third, extract the repeated logic into a single function, module, or service. Make the new abstraction small and focused to keep it readable. Fourth, replace callers with the new representation and run tests. Fifth, review the abstraction for clarity and document the authoritative location. A concrete example: duplicates of email validation appear across three handlers. Name it "validate email format," write tests for expected valid and invalid inputs, extract a single validate_email function, and replace the three implementations with calls to it. A common pitfall is extracting too much responsibility into one abstraction. Keep single responsibility in mind and prefer small focused functions. The final step should include a short code review to ensure the abstraction reads naturally to future maintainers. A Refactoring Process to Remove Duplication means detect → test → extract → replace → review. tests and small focused abstractions reduce risk.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Refactoring Process

Step-by-step refactor

1
Detect and name
Describe the repeated knowledge in one sentence. This name becomes the abstraction's contract.
2
Test current behavior
Capture inputs, expected outputs, and edge cases so refactor safety is measured by passing tests.
3
Extract small abstraction
Keep it focused. Avoid bundling unrelated responsibilities into one function or class.
4
Replace and verify
Replace callers with the new representation and run tests and a code review.
Concrete example
Email validation: write tests for valid and invalid addresses, extract validate_email, replace all handlers, and re-run tests. The single validator becomes the rule source.
Key Takeaway

Tests and small abstractions make DRY refactors safe and maintainable.

screens.title: Before: Duplicated Validation Logic
screens.subtitle: Examine the repeated checks that motivate refactoring

narration.text: Let's walk through a concrete 'before' example that shows duplicated validation logic and why it causes maintenance pain. In the sample, two functions check username, email, and password rules independently. The immediate problem is obvious: the same rule appears in multiple places. The cost emerges when a rule changes — for example, if password complexity increases — and some sites forget to update one handler. That creates inconsistent behavior for users and bugs that are hard to detect. When you inspect duplicated code, look for common structure, identical condition checks, and repeated error messages. Before extracting, write tests that capture current behavior: valid cases, invalid formats, and boundary lengths. A misconception is assuming small duplications are harmless because they are short; even short repeated checks create technical debt. In the next slide you'll see the refactored version that centralizes the checks into validate_username, validate_email, and validate_password functions. That refactor reduces surface area for future changes. In practical terms, examine the repeated checks that motivate refactoring. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Before: Duplication

Before: duplicated validation

BEFORE (Python)
def register_user(username, email, password):
    if not username or len(username) < 3:
        raise ValueError("Username must be at least 3 characters.")
    if "@" not in email or "." not in email:
        raise ValueError("Invalid email format.")
    if len(password) < 8 or not any(char.isdigit() for char in password):
        raise ValueError("Password must be at least 8 characters and contain a digit.")
    # ... actual registration logic ...


def update_user_profile(user_id, new_email, new_password):
    # ... retrieve user ...
    if "@" not in new_email or "." not in new_email: # Duplication!
        raise ValueError("Invalid email format.")
    if len(new_password) < 8 or not any(char.isdigit() for char in new_password): # Duplication!
        raise ValueError("Password must be at least 8 characters and contain a digit.")
    # ... actual update logic ...
Why this is problematic
  • Change in a validation rule requires multiple edits across functions.
  • Tests may miss one of the implementations, leaving inconsistent behavior.
  • Duplicated error messages and logic increase cognitive load for maintainers.
Check your understanding

What tests would you write to capture the current behavior before refactoring?

screens.title: After: Centralized Validation
screens.subtitle: Extracted functions become the single source of truth

narration.text: Here is the 'after' refactor that centralizes validation into three small functions. The advantage is clear: a single place to implement validation rules and to audit security or policy changes. Extracted functions should be intentionally simple: validate_username, validate_email, and validate_password. Callers simply invoke the validators and proceed with core logic, which reduces duplicated branches and repeated error strings. Tests now target the validators directly and the higher level functions can use a small number of integration tests to ensure end-to-end behavior. A misconception is that abstraction makes code slower to navigate. In practice, meaningful names and small focused functions make code easier to read because intent is explicit. If later a rule diverges for a specific context, the centralized function can be safely extended or a new specialized function introduced. The important habit is to centralize knowledge that truly represents the same rule and to test that rule independently. After: Centralized Validation means central validators provide a single place to change rules and a focused test surface for correctness.. In practical terms, extracted functions become the single source of truth. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › After: Centralized Validation

After: Extracted validators

AFTER (Python)
def validate_email(email):
    if "@" not in email or "." not in email:
        raise ValueError("Invalid email format.")


def validate_password(password):
    if len(password) < 8 or not any(char.isdigit() for char in password):
        raise ValueError("Password must be at least 8 characters and contain a digit.")


def validate_username(username):
    if not username or len(username) < 3:
        raise ValueError("Username must be at least 3 characters.")


def register_user_dry(username, email, password):
    validate_username(username)
    validate_email(email)
    validate_password(password)
    # ... actual registration logic ...
Why this helps
  • Single place to update validation rules and messages.
  • Focused unit tests for each validator reduce duplicated test code.
  • Callers are simpler and express intent clearly by calling named validators.
Key Takeaway

Meaningful, small abstractions reduce the surface area of change and improve auditability.

screens.title: Abstraction Patterns for DRY
screens.subtitle: Functions, modules, services and where to place the authoritative knowledge

narration.text: When you refactor to remove duplication, choose an abstraction that matches the knowledge's scope. Small, local rules typically belong in a utility function or module. Shared business rules used across components may belong to a domain module or a small service. Cross‑cutting concerns like authentication or logging are often best handled with middleware or interceptors, which centralize behavior without coupling business logic. For configuration values, a single loader or repository that knows the canonical keys and conversion rules is appropriate. The practical guideline is single responsibility: the abstraction should encapsulate only that piece of knowledge. For example, authentication checks applied to many endpoints become middleware; storing database connection strings belongs in one config loader. A common mistake is creating giant modules that accumulate unrelated responsibilities. Prefer small, named abstractions and explicit interfaces. Later, if a module grows too big, split it along clear boundaries. Clear names and tests make abstractions self-documenting and easier to maintain. Abstraction Patterns for DRY means pick abstractions that match scope: functions for local rules, modules/services for shared rules, middleware for cross-cutting concerns.. In practical terms, functions, modules, services and where to place the authoritative knowledge. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Pattern selection
keyIdea.text: Pick abstractions that match scope: functions for local rules, modules/services for shared rules, middleware for cross-cutting concerns.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Abstraction Patterns

Choosing the right abstraction

Function / Module
Use for small, focused rules like validators or formatters. Test and name clearly.
Domain Service
For business rules used across features, a domain module or service centralizes logic and state.
Middleware / Interceptor
Cross-cutting concerns like auth and logging belong here to avoid sprinkling checks across handlers.
Configuration loader pattern

Centralize the knowledge of which settings exist and how to convert them. A loader merges defaults, environment, and user overrides into one authoritative config object.

Pro Tip

Keep abstractions small and well-named. If a future divergence occurs, splitting a named abstraction is easier than undoing a tangled one.

screens.title: Middleware Example: Centralizing Auth Checks
screens.subtitle: How middleware prevents repeating authorization logic across routes

narration.text: Authorization and authentication checks are a classic cross‑cutting concern that benefits from centralization. When every route handler repeats the same checks, you duplicate knowledge and increase risk. Instead, create a middleware or interceptor that enforces the rule once for all relevant endpoints. The middleware knows the authoritative policy: how to extract identity from a request, how to validate credentials, and which roles are required. Handlers then assume they receive an authenticated context and focus on business behavior. A concrete benefit is easier audits: reviewing the middleware shows who has access and where to change policies. A common misstep is putting too much business logic into middleware. Keep middleware limited to cross-cutting concerns and return clear error responses. Tests should validate both middleware behavior and that handlers receive the expected authenticated context. This pattern reduces duplication, centralizes security concerns, and makes it easier to update authorization rules over time. Middleware Example: Centralizing Auth Checks means centralize cross-cutting checks to reduce repetition and make security policies auditable and maintainable.. In practical terms, how middleware prevents repeating authorization logic across routes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Middleware advantage
keyIdea.text: Centralize cross-cutting checks to reduce repetition and make security policies auditable and maintainable.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Middleware Example

Middleware for Authentication and Authorization

Pattern
  1. Extract auth logic to middleware that validates tokens or sessions.
  2. Attach an authenticated context to the request object.
  3. Handlers rely on the context and do not re-check credentials.
  4. Change policy in one place and tests exercise middleware behaviors.
Concrete scenario

If password reset, profile update, and admin routes each re-checked permissions, central middleware reduces code and provides a single test surface for access rules.

Key Takeaway

Middleware centralizes cross-cutting knowledge and lowers the chance of inconsistent access rules.

screens.title: Premature Abstraction vs. Practical DRY
screens.subtitle: When to abstract and when to wait

narration.text: Not every repeated-looking code should be abstracted immediately. Premature abstraction happens when you create a generalized solution before you understand the variations that will appear. This often leads to conditional logic, special cases, or a leaky abstraction. The pragmatic approach is to ask whether the duplication represents the same piece of knowledge or only accidental similarity. One rule of thumb is to wait until you see a third occurrence before creating a broad abstraction, or to create a small, obvious helper with a clear name that can be expanded later. A concrete contrast: two functions that sort lists for different domains may look identical now but will probably diverge — avoid bundling them prematurely. A common misconception is that DRY always requires immediate extraction; instead, prioritize clarity. If you do extract, prefer narrow interfaces and good tests so that if divergence occurs, you can split the abstraction cleanly. Premature Abstraction vs. Practical DRY means don't abstract before you understand the knowledge. prefer small, testable helpers and watch for real repetition patterns.. In practical terms, when to abstract and when to wait. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: When to wait
keyIdea.text: Don't abstract before you understand the knowledge. Prefer small, testable helpers and watch for real repetition patterns.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Premature Abstraction

Premature Abstraction vs Practical DRY

Premature abstraction

Happens when an abstraction bundles unrelated behavior or anticipates future differences. It can create complexity and conditional logic.

Warning

Clever abstractions that save a few lines today may cost clarity tomorrow.

Practical DRY

Favor small, named helpers and tests. Wait for evidence of repeated patterns or use incremental refactors you can split later.

Checklist

Is the repetition the same knowledge? Are tests in place? Can the abstraction be small and clear?

screens.title: Refactor the Configuration Loader (Starter Code)
screens.subtitle: Centralize which settings exist and how they convert

narration.text: For a hands-on exercise, refactor the configuration loader to remove duplicated merging logic. The original code has separate functions that iterate over known keys and parse values from environment and user files. Notice both functions repeat the same mapping and conversion steps. The task is to create a helper that encodes the canonical keys and conversion rules, and then reuse it in the environment and file loaders. This centralizes the knowledge of which settings exist and how to convert types, such as turning a string into an integer for max connections. Start by listing the canonical keys and desired types. Then implement a helper that, given a source mapping, returns processed settings with conversions applied. Replace the two loaders to call that helper rather than duplicating the logic. Tests should validate defaults, environment overrides, and user file overrides. A good refactor keeps the A P I the same while making the merging logic easy to inspect and change. Refactor the Configuration Loader (Starter Code) means encapsulate settings metadata and conversion rules so multiple loaders reuse the same knowledge.. In practical terms, centralize which settings exist and how they convert. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Config Loader Exercise

Starter code — refactor task

Starter Code (Python)
import os

def load_default_config():
    default_settings = {
        "DATABASE_URL": "sqlite:///app.db",
        "LOG_LEVEL": "INFO",
        "MAX_CONNECTIONS": 10
    }
    print("Loaded default config.")
    return default_settings


def load_env_config():
    env_settings = {}
    if "APP_DATABASE_URL" in os.environ:
        env_settings["DATABASE_URL"] = os.environ["APP_DATABASE_URL"]
    if "APP_LOG_LEVEL" in os.environ:
        env_settings["LOG_LEVEL"] = os.environ["APP_LOG_LEVEL"]
    if "APP_MAX_CONNECTIONS" in os.environ:
        env_settings["MAX_CONNECTIONS"] = int(os.environ["APP_MAX_CONNECTIONS"])
    print("Loaded environment config.")
    return env_settings
Refactor guidance
  1. Define a canonical metadata map: key name, env var name, conversion function.
  2. Implement a helper that applies conversions for a given source mapping.
  3. Use the helper in load_env_config and load_user_override_config to avoid duplicated loops.
  4. Write tests for defaults, env overrides, and user file parsing.
Check

Does the helper encode which settings exist and how to convert them? If yes, you have centralized knowledge.

screens.title: Assessment: Spot and Fix a DRY Violation
screens.subtitle: Questions and a rubric for evaluating refactors

narration.text: Assessment should measure whether learners can find duplication, name the underlying knowledge, and perform a safe refactor. Present a code snippet with similar but slightly different functions and ask the learner whether the repetition is the same knowledge. A correct answer explains whether to extract and which abstraction to use, and lists tests needed to make the change safe. A rubric includes: detection (did the student find repetitions?), naming (did they clearly state the knowledge in one sentence?), refactoring plan (tests + extraction steps), and final verification (unit and integration tests pass). For example, a question could present three handlers each with their own email checks and ask: is this a DRY violation and how would you refactor it? A strong response extracts a shared validator, provides tests for valid and invalid inputs, and updates handlers to call the validator. Weak responses either ignore the knowledge level or propose an overly complex abstraction. The goal is practical correctness, not cleverness. Assessment: Spot and Fix a DRY Violation means evaluate detection, naming, refactor plan, and test coverage to confirm knowledge centralization.. In practical terms, questions and a rubric for evaluating refactors. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Let's summarize the key concepts to carry forward. First, DRY demands a single authoritative representation of knowledge, not merely removal of duplicated lines. Second, duplication can be syntactic, knowledge-based, data-driven, or process-oriented, and each type has a distinct remedy. Third, refactoring to remove duplication should be guided by tests and small, focused abstractions to avoid introducing brittle or overly clever solutions. These ideas together help you reduce bugs, simplify updates, and make audits easier. As you return to your codebase, look for repeated intent and ask: where should this rule live? That question will guide practical improvements without over-abstraction. Keep the checklist of detect, test, extract, replace, and review handy as a repeatable workflow for safe refactors. Key Concepts means dry is about authoritative knowledge. use tests and small abstractions to centralize rules safely.. In practical terms, what to remember from this chapter. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Summary
keyIdea.text: DRY is about authoritative knowledge. Use tests and small abstractions to centralize rules safely.

Distinguish between syntactic similarity and shared knowledge before abstracting.
Refactor Safely
Detect, test, extract, replace, and review — testing makes DRY refactors safe.
Takeaway

Centralize knowledge where it belongs. Prefer small, tested abstractions and avoid premature generalization.

narration.text: Finish with a compact checklist you can use during code review. First, name the repeated behavior. Second, check if repeated code represents the same knowledge. Third, write tests that capture the current behavior before changing anything. Fourth, extract a small, focused abstraction with a clear name. Fifth, replace callers and run tests. Sixth, avoid coupling unrelated responsibilities into one abstraction; split when needed. These reminders help you apply DRY pragmatically: reduce duplication that harms changeability while preserving clarity. When in doubt, prefer a readable helper and tests over an early, complex generalization. The result is a codebase that adapts to change with fewer bugs and clearer intent. Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Quick Reminders

Quick DRY Reminders

1. Name it
Describe the repeated knowledge in one clear sentence.
2. Test it
Capture behavior so refactors are safe and verifiable.
3. Keep it small
Prefer focused helpers and avoid heavy generalization early.
Final Thought

DRY is not an aesthetic rule; it's a tool to keep systems consistent and maintainable. Use it with judgment and tests.
